def: A single action an agent takes on something outside the conversation, such as reading a file, writing a file, running a command, or fetching a page.
pitfall: Counting a long stretch of agent narration as work; only tool calls change anything, so a run that explains a great deal and calls few tools has mostly been talking to itself.
distractor_rationale: People arriving from chat assistants read fluent text as the product, because in chat the text genuinely was the product.

def: What comes back to the agent from an action it took: file contents, an error, a list of results. It is information the agent did not have when the task was handed over.
pitfall: Treating an error in the feedback as a failed run, when adapting to errors is precisely how an agent learns what is actually true about your files.
distractor_rationale: Errors read as malfunctions to anyone whose experience of software is that a red message means something broke.

def: The cycle of calling a tool, reading what came back, and choosing the next call — the property that makes a system an agent rather than a script.
pitfall: Assuming the loop follows a plan fixed at the start, when each iteration's choice depends on feedback that did not exist when you wrote the task.
distractor_rationale: Anyone who has used an automation or macro expects a recorded sequence, so they picture a list of steps being replayed rather than decided.

def: One span of the tool-calling loop, from the task you hand over to the moment it stops.
pitfall: Thinking of a run as one long chat message; a run leaves changed files behind whether or not you ever read its report.
distractor_rationale: The interface often looks like a chat window, so the mental model carries over from a surface that could not touch anything.

def: One message-and-reply exchange with no tool-calling loop in it, where anything that happens in the real world happens because you did it.
pitfall: Assuming the same request is equally safe in both modes, when a chat turn's worst outcome is a bad paragraph and a run's is a changed file.
distractor_rationale: The request text is often word-for-word identical in both, so the difference lives entirely in what the system is permitted to do with it.

def: A system where the steps are fixed in advance by code and the model fills in the blanks, as distinct from an agent that chooses its own steps.
pitfall: Calling every multi-step AI system an agent, which hides that a fixed-step system is predictable in exactly the way an agent is not.
distractor_rationale: Marketing applies the word agent to both, so learners never encounter the distinction until an unpredictable run makes it concrete.

def: Handing over a task along with the authority to take the intermediate steps unsupervised.
pitfall: Delegating a task you could not grade afterwards, which buys you a result you have no way to judge rather than time saved.
distractor_rationale: Tedium feels like the natural signal for what to hand off, and the most tedious tasks are often the ones whose output is hardest to check.

def: The property that each action changes the situation the next action starts from, so a run accumulates consequences as it goes.
pitfall: Expecting a failed run to leave things as they were; a run that stops halfway leaves half its changes in place.
distractor_rationale: Familiar software either completes or rolls back, so partial permanent change is not a state most people have had to reason about.

def: A mistake whose cost grows because later work is built on top of it.
pitfall: Estimating the damage from the wrong step alone, rather than from everything the run did afterwards on that basis.
distractor_rationale: In a chat, a wrong answer is self-contained and costs nothing to discard, so the habit of bounding a mistake to where it occurred transfers badly.

def: An action you could undo in about a minute if it turned out wrong — creating a file, writing a draft, reading something.
pitfall: Classifying an action as reversible because undoing it is theoretically possible, without checking whether you would actually notice in time to do it.
distractor_rationale: Reversibility feels like a property of the action, when in practice it depends on whether a copy of the original still exists.

def: An action whose undoing is expensive or impossible: deleting, sending to another person, overwriting an original with no copy, or changing something others depend on.
pitfall: Listing only deletion, and missing that sending a message or overwriting the sole copy of a file is equally unrecoverable.
distractor_rationale: Deletion is the vivid case, so it crowds out the quieter ones that produce the same permanent result.

def: The sequence of tool calls a run actually made, in order, with what came back from each — a record of events rather than a description of them.
pitfall: Reading the trail only after something has visibly gone wrong, when its main value is catching runs whose summary looks entirely fine.
distractor_rationale: The summary is presented as the run's conclusion, so the trail reads as debugging output for problems rather than the primary evidence.

def: Four questions asked before handing over a task: is it multi-step, can you check the result, what is the worst irreversible action in reach, and could you tell a good result from a plausible one.
pitfall: Answering the fourth question optimistically; if you could not spot a convincing wrong answer, the run cannot teach you anything when it fails.
distractor_rationale: The first three questions have crisp answers, which makes the fourth feel like a formality rather than the one that decides the outcome.

def: The set of decisions you state explicitly — done, work area, gates, stopping condition — so the agent does not silently supply its own values for them.
pitfall: Writing the boundary as tone rather than as values, so instructions like 'be careful' leave every actual threshold still unspecified.
distractor_rationale: Cautionary language feels protective, and it reads to a person as a real constraint even though it contains nothing checkable.

def: A finish line stated so the agent can test its own work against it, rather than deciding for itself when the task feels complete.
pitfall: Omitting what should happen to items the agent cannot handle, which turns every skipped item into silence indistinguishable from success.
distractor_rationale: Describing the successful outcome feels like a complete specification, because the failure cases have not happened yet when you write it.

def: What the agent is technically able to reach at all, as distinct from what it is permitted to do without asking.
pitfall: Leaving the work area at whatever the tool defaults to, so an agent searching for something it needs can wander into folders you never considered.
distractor_rationale: A default that has never caused a problem reads as a safe default, since the reach you did not want is invisible until it is exercised.

def: How far the consequences of a wrong action can spread, which is bounded by the work area rather than by the agent's intentions.
pitfall: Judging blast radius from what the task requires rather than from what the agent can reach, when the second is what an overeager step will actually find.
distractor_rationale: People reason from the task's scope because that is what they were thinking about when they wrote the request.

def: A point where the agent must stop and ask you before proceeding with something it is otherwise able to do.
pitfall: Gating every action, which produces so many prompts that you approve them without reading and end up with less oversight than a few well-chosen gates.
distractor_rationale: More checkpoints feels monotonically safer, because the model of attention as unlimited is never explicitly examined.

def: In OpenAI's Codex documentation, the control governing what the agent can do technically, including where it can write and whether it can reach the network.
pitfall: Conflating it with the approval policy, when one limits capability and the other only decides when the agent must pause and ask.
distractor_rationale: Both feel like the single dial labelled how much freedom to give it, so the two-axis structure collapses into one in most people's heads.

def: In OpenAI's Codex documentation, the control governing when the agent must ask you before it executes an action.
pitfall: Relying on approval prompts as the only protection, when an action outside the work area should be impossible rather than merely announced.
distractor_rationale: Being asked feels like control, and it is — but only for as long as you are still reading the questions carefully.

def: A run taking an action that is plausibly connected to its task but reaches past what the person intended to authorize.
pitfall: Looking for obviously wrong actions, when the documented cases look like reasonable problem-solving applied too broadly.
distractor_rationale: The word escalation suggests something dramatic, so a sensible-looking action at the wrong scale does not match the mental image.

def: A limit that ends a run regardless of whether the task is finished — a step ceiling, a time budget, or a rule such as stopping after the same error twice.
pitfall: Assuming a stuck run will give up on its own, when an agent that cannot finish will keep attempting and each attempt costs you something.
distractor_rationale: Programs that hang are familiar, but agents narrate while they struggle, so the activity reads as progress rather than as a loop.

def: The length of task an agent completes at a given success rate; METR's 50% time horizon is the duration at which an agent is predicted to succeed half the time.
pitfall: Treating any published horizon figure as a current capability, when the measurement is tied to a model generation and a task suite and moves quickly.
distractor_rationale: A single number invites use as a specification, which is exactly how it stops being true a few months after it is published.

def: An agent trying to complete a whole task in a single sweep rather than in checkpointed pieces, leaving nothing to resume from if it fails partway.
pitfall: Judging it by whether the final output looks complete, when the real cost appears only when the run dies at eighty percent with no intermediate state saved.
distractor_rationale: A run that produces everything at the end looks efficient, since incremental output is invisible while the run is succeeding.

def: A report of success from a run that never verified the work — indistinguishable from a genuine completion report by inspection alone.
pitfall: Asking the agent to double-check, which returns a second statement from the same source rather than independent evidence.
distractor_rationale: Asking again is what works with a person who might have been careless, and the interface makes the agent feel like such a person.

def: The accumulated working memory of a run — everything it has read and done so far — which fills as the run proceeds.
pitfall: Expecting step forty of a run to be executed as reliably as step four, when coherence degrades as the context fills.
distractor_rationale: Software is normally as accurate on its thousandth operation as its first, so gradual within-run degradation has no familiar analogue.

def: Anthropic's term for models beginning to wrap up work prematurely as they approach what they believe is their context limit.
pitfall: Trusting the end of a long run most, when the closing stretch — where completion claims are made — is the least reliable part of it.
distractor_rationale: A conclusion normally reflects everything that came before, so the final summary intuitively feels like the most informed statement in the run.

def: A run's continued grip on its original goal and accumulated state, which vendors report degrades over lengthy tasks.
pitfall: Reading a loss of coherence as the agent misunderstanding the task, when it understood correctly at the start and lost the thread over distance.
distractor_rationale: Misunderstanding is the familiar explanation for wrong output, so people rewrite the instruction when the real fix is a shorter run.

def: The check asking whether a run touched everything it was supposed to touch, answered by counting actions in the trail against the items requested.
pitfall: Skipping it because it feels too crude, when counting catches more incomplete runs than any amount of reading the output does.
distractor_rationale: Counting feels beneath the sophistication of the problem, so people go straight to inspecting content quality instead.

def: The check asking whether the run looked at the result of its own changes, visible as read-back actions following write actions in the trail.
pitfall: Mistaking a tool reporting success for the agent verifying an outcome; the first says the command ran, not that it did what was wanted.
distractor_rationale: An ok in the trail after every action reads as confirmation, because it is the same word a person would use to confirm.

def: The check for things that failed without leaving a note — the hardest gap to see, because you are looking for something that is not there.
pitfall: Assuming problems announce themselves, when an agent with nowhere to record a failure will guess or move on quietly.
distractor_rationale: Absence carries no visual weight in a log, so a missing entry never draws the eye the way an error message does.

def: The check for whether a run touched anything outside its declared work area.
pitfall: Checking only the files the task named, and missing the directory listings and searches that show where the agent looked.
distractor_rationale: Reading and listing feel harmless next to writing, so exploratory actions get skipped when scanning a trail.

def: A short artifact stating what a run was asked to do, what it actually did, what you personally verified, and what remains open.
pitfall: Filling the verified section with the agent's claims instead of your own checks, which collapses the distinction the record exists to preserve.
distractor_rationale: Both kinds of statement describe the same work in the same past tense, so the difference in their evidential weight is easy to lose while writing.

def: GitHub's term for the record showing an agent's reasoning and the tools it used, linked from each commit so a change can be traced during review or audit.
pitfall: Treating it as a debugging tool for failed runs, when its documented purpose is routine review of runs that appear to have succeeded.
distractor_rationale: The word log signals troubleshooting, so it gets opened only when something has already gone visibly wrong.

def: A record written as events occur and never rewritten, which is why it can be checked against a summary composed afterwards.
pitfall: Substituting the agent's own recap of what it did, which is reconstructed from the same beliefs that produced the summary you are trying to check.
distractor_rationale: A recap is easier to read than a raw trail, and it appears to contain the same information in a friendlier form.

def: The limited supply of careful looking a person has during a run, which is smaller than the number of moments competing for it.
pitfall: Spending it evenly across a run, which leaves nothing for the one decision that actually mattered.
distractor_rationale: Vigilance is experienced as a matter of will, so treating it as a finite quantity to allocate feels like making an excuse.

def: Anthropic's term for people ceasing to pay close attention to what they are approving after repeated prompts.
pitfall: Responding to a near-miss by adding more prompts, which accelerates the fatigue that let the near-miss through.
distractor_rationale: Adding a checkpoint is the standard fix after any process failure, and it works for processes that do not depend on a human reading each one.

def: The signal of the same action against the same target with the same result, indicating a run that is circling rather than gathering information.
pitfall: Confusing it with retrying, when a second attempt that differs from the first is recovery and only an identical repeat is circling.
distractor_rationale: Both look like doing the same thing twice at a glance, and the difference sits in the detail of the action rather than in its shape.

def: The signal of a run beginning to touch things adjacent to its task rather than in it — scope escalation observed live, before it completes.
pitfall: Waiting to see what it does with the wider material, when this is the last cheap moment to stop before an irreversible step.
distractor_rationale: The agent usually narrates a plausible reason for looking further afield, which makes waiting feel like fairness rather than delay.

def: The signal of actions continuing while nothing is produced or written, readable directly when a task was set up to write output as it goes.
pitfall: Reading visible activity as progress, when the useful measure is whether the output is still growing rather than whether the run is still moving.
distractor_rationale: A scrolling display is the universal sign that something is working, so stillness in the output goes unnoticed beneath the motion.

def: The signal of narration reporting progress the actions do not show — a premature completion claim caught while the run is still going.
pitfall: Taking a confident progress statement as a checkpoint, when the trail may show no action since the last failure.
distractor_rationale: Confident phrasing is how people signal they have verified something, so the register carries an assurance the run never earned.

def: The response of letting a run proceed, correct when it is converging: index advancing, output growing, failures landing in the record.
pitfall: Continuing on the strength of the agent sounding confident rather than on the observable markers of convergence.
distractor_rationale: Interrupting feels disruptive and rude, so any reassuring narration is welcomed as grounds to leave it alone.

def: Correcting a run without ending it — supplying a missing fact or narrowing the target — so the work already done survives.
pitfall: Forgetting it exists and treating every concern as a stop-or-continue choice, which throws away good work over a fixable misdirection.
distractor_rationale: The visible controls are usually stop and approve, so the middle option is not represented in the interface even where it is supported.

def: Ending a run and completing the work yourself, correct when repetition persists after a redirect, when something irreversible is near, or when the task itself was mis-specified.
pitfall: Redirecting once more when the run is already exploring outside its work area, where the cost of being wrong is an action you cannot undo.
distractor_rationale: Sunk effort makes stopping feel wasteful, and one more correction always looks cheaper than starting over.

def: Verifying a sample of a run's output by hand against its source, and recording how many items you actually checked.
pitfall: Reporting a spot-check as though it covered everything, rather than naming the sample size so the unverified remainder stays visible.
distractor_rationale: Finding no problems in a sample feels like evidence about the whole, which is exactly the inference the recorded count is there to prevent.

def: An action that reads a destination after writing to it, confirming the change landed rather than assuming the write succeeded.
pitfall: Assuming a run verified its work because the trail is long, when a trail of writes with no reads confirmed nothing at all.
distractor_rationale: Volume of activity reads as thoroughness, and the distinction between writing and checking is invisible unless you look at action types.

def: Results written as the run proceeds rather than summarized at the end, so a run that dies partway still leaves usable work behind.
pitfall: Accepting an end-of-run summary as equivalent, when it is composed after the fact from the same memory that may already be wrong.
distractor_rationale: A single tidy report looks more organized than a running log, so the format that is easier to read displaces the one that is evidence.

def: A boundary requirement that anything skipped, ambiguous, or unreadable be reported explicitly, converting a silence into a line you can find.
pitfall: Requiring reports only for things the agent could not do, and leaving no channel for things it did badly on a low-confidence guess.
distractor_rationale: Outright failures are the obvious case to plan for, while uncertain successes look identical to confident ones in the output.

def: The point in a task where the work changes character — gathering to deciding, reading to writing — which is where a long task should be split.
pitfall: Splitting by volume instead, which halves the item count while leaving each half just as dependent on unverified work from the other.
distractor_rationale: Cutting a task in half is the obvious way to make it smaller, and it does reduce length without creating anything checkable in between.

def: An observation that looks alarming but does not justify interrupting — most importantly, a run encountering errors and adapting to them.
pitfall: Stopping runs at the first error, which discards a working delegation and teaches you nothing about what real failure looks like.
distractor_rationale: Error text is visually alarming and formatted like a problem, whether the run is failing or successfully learning what is there.

def: A file a run updates as it works, so a later session or reader can tell what was genuinely completed instead of inferring it from the state of the work.
pitfall: Relying on the visible state of the work instead, which is the exact inference that led a documented agent to see progress and declare the job done.
distractor_rationale: Finished-looking work is tangible evidence, and it is genuinely evidence of something — just not of the task being complete.

def: A gating pattern that requires approval for the first few instances of an action and then proceeds unattended once the pattern is confirmed.
pitfall: Preferring uniform gates because they feel more thorough, when approval quality collapses long before a uniform gate stops firing.
distractor_rationale: Consistency reads as rigour, so a rule applied to every case looks stronger than one deliberately concentrated where judgment still works.
